I really didn’t like the story either. The whole premise revolves around a selfish kid who only decides to care for his grandmother at the end of her life because he wants her inheritance. Personally, inheritance has never meant much to me, but using family like that is just wrong—especially exploiting your own grandmother. The character’s “growth” is basically him learning to love her, which shouldn’t even be a lesson in the first place. Grandmothers are usually the one person you love unconditionally (unless there’s a bad relationship). Because of his initial motives, I couldn’t connect with any of the emotional moments. I also found him extremely unlikable. He just feels like a frustrating main character overall. Bruh you should help your mom not your grandmother... There’s also no real chemistry among the cast. On top of everything, there’s this strange subplot involving cousin incest that feels unnecessary and uncomfortable. I genuinely don’t understand why it was included. It also seems like the director thinks adding random piano music to every scene automatically makes it emotional, which it doesn’t. I expected a story about a kid trying to earn money to help his grandmother before she passes away not someone taking advantage of her for personal gain. Yes, watching a grandmother die is naturally sad, but that alone doesn’t make the movie good. OVERRATED FILM

Om det er noget kultur jeg ikke kan sætte mig ind i, ved jeg ikke lige. Den har da nogle fornuftige momenter, og normalt er jeg ikke bleg for at give mig hen til de helst store følelser, men jeg var der bare ikke her. Hele præmissen med en familie, der i udgangspunktet er totalt splittet, hvorefter det usympatiske barnebarn pludselig ændrer kurs for at finde tilbage til sin døende bedstemor, føltes utrolig manipulerende og uægte. Det hjalp heller ikke, at man proppede alt muligt fyld som en tyvagtig onkel ind i ligningen. Filmen trak i det hele taget i langdrag; den skar ud i pap i en uendelighed, i stedet for rent faktisk at give os tid til at mærke den dybere relation. Det var bl.a. her den havde sine momentvise gode ting. Når mormor og M “fandt hinanden” igennem samtale. Jeg var også glad for replikken der omhandlede hvordan gamle menneskers hjem lugter og man først har tilbragt nok tid hos dem, når man ikke længere lægger mærke til det. Jeg havde egentlig også sympati for, hvordan filmen udstiller det problematiske i, at sønner ofte render med arven, mens døtre løfter den tunge opgave, som primære omsorgspersoner for de ældre forældre – hvilket nok gør sig gældende i mange kulturer. Alt i alt, er der bare for mange uoverensstemmelser og mærkelige sidespor i historien og jeg har svært ved at gennemskue, om det er en integreret del af fortællingen, eller om det bare er drysset henover som krymmel. Hjertet er uden tvivl på det rette sted, men filmen drukner i sin egen manipulation, ikke mindst med det enerverende score.

I’m probably the only person who didn’t cry during this movie, mostly because I was busy taking a nap. I fell asleep halfway through and honestly, my brain just checked out. I get that this is a massive hit for people who want a "good cry," but for me, it felt more like an endurance test in emotional manipulation. Maybe it’s because I actually have a healthy relationship with my family? The whole premise of treating a grandmother like a strategic asset or a bank account feels so alien and cynical that I couldn't find a way into the story. If you don't have that specific baggage of a fractured, transactional family life, the "tension" here just feels like people being unnecessarily difficult. It’s hard to stay awake for a reconciliation that shouldn't be this hard in the first place. Technically, the movie is paying a heavy "sadness tax." Every time those slow piano chords kick in, it’s like the director is tapping you on the shoulder saying, “Okay, start crying now. This is the sad part.” I value restraint and emotional honesty where the stakes feel earned. This felt like the opposite. It doesn't earn its emotions; it demands them through pacing that is slow enough to be a sedative. The acting is solid, and I can see why people like it, but it’s just not for me. I’d much rather watch experts being competent at their jobs or a story that subverts tropes instead of leaning into them this hard. If you need to clear your sinuses with a tactical tear-jerker, go for it. But if you prefer a movie that respects your intelligence without spoon-feeding you the "feels," you might end up catching some Z’s like I did. The Verdict: A well-made sedative. Great if you need a cry, even better if you need a nap.

The only things really preventing this from being completely sacchrine, overly sentimental tripe are some stellar performances (particularly by the grandmother) and beautiful cinematography (which is mostly helped along by the natural beauty of Thailand). The central characters do feel like fully realized individuals, which makes the central theme of fraught and complex family relationships impactful. But at the end of the day, its just the same perpetual fantasy of the older generation under capitalism that the younger generation will learn the value of hard work, familial piety, and tradition, despite the alienating force of capital, which turns all relationships into transactions. I think what makes something like Parasite feel more honest, despite its surrealism (or heightened realism?), is that it doesn't shy away from that reality or try to sugarcoat it. There is a potentially much more interesting movie here with a reworked ending and a few minor adjustments to the story. But as it is, its just way too sentimental for me.

Accept what cannot be changed. Discovering that there is money to made in looking after elderly folks who will write you into their will, a college dropout starts spending time with his cancer-ridden grandmother in this sentimental drama from Thailand. The idea of taking care of senior citizens with cunning ulterior motives is intriguing, but the film is more focus on the grandmother/grandson bond. The movie has a considerable fanbase and there is certainly something sweet in how gradually comes to appreciate his grandmother for more than just her money. All such character growth is telegraphed so far in advance though that it is hard to sit through over two hours of fluff just to see him reach an obvious conclusion about what matters in life. The film is also beset from one of the most cloying and maudlin music scores in recent memory. While the character growth in the film is predictable, the movie admittedly goes in some unexpected directions in its second half, but with a few too many false endings before the actual conclusion arrives, it is hard to say that the film ends on a strong note. It is also a bit irksome how the grandmother's cancer diagnosis is used as a plot device with the film uninterested in exploring how the condition impacts her; it is not even until the second half of the film that we discover what type of cancer it is. With solid performances all round, particularly from Usha Seamkhum as the dying woman who always suspects what others are not prepared to tell her, the appeal of the movie is easy to see, but Bad Genius is far better option for those wanting to check Thailand off their Letterboxd World Map.

love can be extraction. we love for reciprocation, perform care to solicit reward — monetary, social, and psychological. but to suggest that we love purely out of selfishness is to ignore the ache of grief, the jubilance of laughter, and the harmony of imperfect togetherness. perhaps we love so much that we ache to be loved back unselfishly, we don’t want to be taken care of if it is predicated on reciprocity, protection, and loyalty. in wanting this we misconstrue the care of those who love us most — those who selfishly extract love from us as we do love from them. everyone is implicated in the economy of affection. love involves exchange which may you leave you feeling indebted, expectant, or fraudulent. if love exists in the material world, burdened by material interests, can it ever transcend material incentives? if love is entangled with obligation and inheritance, can it ever be legitimate in the absence of reward? perhaps imperfectly reciprocal love is not saliently deceitful.

Como toda boa garotinha criada por vó, qualquer história sobre velhice e vovós fofas me faz chorar. Então minhas expectativas estavam muito altas pra esse filme. A premissa é interessante: um rapaz, folgado, interesseiro e mal educado, decide cuidar da sua avó doente por puro interesse, na esperança de que ela lhe deixe alguns bens quando morrer. Mais um filme sobre o arco de redenção do protagonista detestável, pensei. Plot batidíssimo, mas emocionante, pensei. O filme é triste, claro. Uma velhinha adorável enfrentando um câncer terminal e a solidão, com familiares detestáveis a seu redor. Acontece que o filme não faz mais que o mínimo ao emocionar. Ele se escora no sentimentalismo do espectador, que certamente vai lembrar de sua própria avó e sentir saudades ou, se viva for, se apegar ao pavor de perdê-la. Pra se certificar do choro da audiência, é adicionada uma trilha sonora de piano emocionante ao fundo. Além do choro, sobra muito pouco: a atuação da vovó, que sem dúvidas é o ponto alto do filme, e algumas reflexões que provavelmente você já teve na vida se você tem mais de 13 anos e já entendeu como a vida funciona. A tão prometida redenção do personagem é intempestiva, abrupta e forçada. Não convence, já que o protagonista passa 80% do filme esperando pela herança ou de birra por não tê-la recebido. No final, usa o dinheiro que a própria avó guardou ao longo dos anos, pra pagar um jazigo bonito e realizar o sonho da velhinha. Convenhamos, isso é o mínimo que um neto minimamente decente faria nessas circunstâncias. Como alguns já falaram na sessão de comentários aqui: não é porque um filme é triste que ele é bom. Esse aqui simplesmente é raso e apelativo.

I kept waiting for this to really get under my skin, but it never quite found a way in. It has plenty to say about family, guilt, and the strange urgency with which we suddenly make time for the people we love when that time is already running out. Some moments genuinely spoke to me, especially the observation that old people only seem to smell because we no longer spend enough time close to them. It’s such a small, unassuming line, yet it carries an uncomfortable truth that’s hard to shake. The story is at its strongest when it explores caregiving and inheritance. The daughters submissively shoulder the burden of looking after ageing parents, putting their own lives on hold without expecting recognition, while the sons remain the natural heirs when it comes time to divide what is left behind. It was heartbreaking seeing the grandmother, despite having lived through that same unfairness, unconsciously reinforce it herself. No one questions it because, in so many cultures, these roles are passed down just as unquestioningly as the inheritance itself. That understanding of family is what makes the final act slightly frustrating. I believed every awkward silence, every petty argument, every buried resentment, and every small act of love that somehow survived beneath it all. But I never believed the grandson’s transformation. I kept waiting for a moment that would fundamentally change the way I saw him, something that would make everything leading up to the ending fall into place. Instead, we’re simply expected to accept that he’s changed without ever really witnessing that change. By the time the credits rolled, I found myself appreciating what the story was trying to do more than what it ultimately achieved.

Lorsqu’il voit qu’une de ses cousines a hérité après s’être occupée de son grand-père, il décide à son tour de se rapprocher de sa grand-mère avec une idée assez simple en tête : devenir son héritier. Évidemment, derrière ce point de départ archi glauque se construit progressivement quelque chose de beaucoup plus humain. Le film dégage une profonde tendresse. On s’attache forcément à cette mamie drôle, énergique, qui taille tout le monde et qui a une sacrée personnalité. Et forcément, la voir décliner petit à petit alors que la relation avec son petit-fils évolue rend l’ensemble de plus en plus touchant. J’ai beaucoup aimé la manière dont cette relation se construit, sans chercher constamment à provoquer l’émotion. Ce sont surtout les petits moments du quotidien, les habitudes, les discussions parfois anodines et le temps passé ensemble qui finissent par donner énormément de valeur à leur histoire. Et derrière cette relation, le film parle très joliment de la famille, du temps qui passe, de ce qu’on donne aux autres et de ce qu’on finit par laisser derrière nous. Il y a quelque chose d’assez universel là-dedans : parfois, on ne réalise vraiment la valeur du temps passé avec quelqu’un que lorsqu’on commence à comprendre qu’il est compté. La fin est très émouvante et vient parfaitement conclure l'oeuvre : Très sympa !
